memories.memory_text: I carried the Milwaukee case past the gravel and cement stacks, heavy on my shoulder, walking with the clerk to buy the hollow core drill—another tool for the job, another step closer to the next safe.
I drilled through the armored plating, cut a clean 10-inch circle, then stepped back and swung up my shotgun as Terry Brooks hit the disc with the sledgehammer.
I told her not to worry about the money—Wesley Thorne’s got it handled, the rest is coming in a couple days. We were already late, and she was stalling.
When she said she wanted out and tried to take Jordan Vaughn, I shoved her against the wall and told her I’d find her and kill her if she ever tried it.

I told Wesley Thorne, 'Lane Finch's going to leave me,' and the words came out flat, like I was still trying to believe it myself. My lip was split, my shirt torn, and my mouth tasted like shit—like last night had finally caught up with me.
I said I'd rather go ten rounds with Jesus Christ than mess with Lane Finch, and meant it—she and Jordan Vaughn are the only thing that keeps me straight, every single day.
I unfolded from the side of the exit gate, shotgun in hand, and fired without hesitation.
I crossed to the Lincoln with Terry Brooks, shotgun in hand, moving clear of the burning pickup while Wesley Thorne finished things with the gunman.
I confirmed the black boxes were delivered by Silverbrook Motel and placed in the drop—alarms were set, ready to go.
I asked what we’d do about Quinn Sterling and then Sage Grayson—two names that needed answers before moving forward.
I asked Lane Finch if she was okay, put my arm around her, and said we were makin’ it happen this time—she just said she hoped so, and for a second, it felt like we were still on the same page.
I took the lock punch out of the case and put it together—felt the weight of it in my hands. Nodded once it was ready.

I moved around the P.G.E. equipment and opened the GTE junction box, then hung the suitcase with the black boxes and clips on the door before starting to trace the colored wires to bypass the alarm circuits.
I felt the tumblers align under my fingers, one by one, and when the fence dropped into place, the door gave way without a sound.
I set up the heavy drill and taped the template to the vault door, marking the drill points—this is where we breach.
I was sixty seconds from cracking the box, the cash almost in reach, but Wesley Thorne said 'We walk,' and I knew it wasn't a choice—I put the tools down.
I didn't recognize the cook at first, just saw him flipping eggs, but when Wesley Thorne mentioned D Block and San Quentin, I remembered the face—Sawyer Hale, ex-con, maybe wired by the cops.
For me, the Pinecrest Hospital's worth the stretch. I say accept the risk, stay.
Wesley Thorne looked at Terry Brooks and said something personal—about Jordan Quincy, about walking away. I didn't expect that from him.
I crouched near the dirt road, sketching the layout of the oil pumps and the access route in the dust with a stick—marking where we’d come in and how we’d get out fast.
I opened my satchel and took out the voltmeter, ready to check the charge—dark as it was, the tearing sound told me Wesley Thorne was already cutting through.
I remember slamming my hand down and asking, 'What the fuck do we do now?' when Silverbrook Motel walked out—suddenly there was no driver, and the job was falling apart.
I told Sawyer Hale the alarms were bypassed last night—no police response, clean entry. This job was supposed to be smooth, just a slow cruise.

I shoved the curved clip into the H&K, felt the bolt slide forward as I jacked the first round into the chamber—cold metal, no room for error. The wagon pulled off the curb, and I kept my hands close, ready.

memories.memory_text: I checked the chamber of my the weathered key, then inserted a 14-shot clip into the grip.
I pulled on the Donald Duck rubber mask—Harper Hollis was putting on a welder’s helmet, same time.
I put Jesse Prescott's envelope on the table and told him to fuck off — he just sat there, frozen, like he didn’t understand what was happening.
I slammed his face into the table and flicked his temple — he was twitching, strung out, and I needed him to feel it before I threw him out.

I told Harper Hollis about Jimmy Banghart’s rule—don’t put anything in your life you can’t walk out on in seconds if you spot heat—because he was too tied to his family, and that makes you vulnerable.
I kicked the waste can aside when she wouldn't answer who the man was—her stumbling over it, backing away like I was the threat.
I told her Harper Hollis gets one more shot—two jobs back-to-back—and if he fails, I’d set her up separately, but she had to give him this chance now.
I looked at the gunman on the ground, his body broken, blood in his mouth, choking. He asked me to do it — I put the the weathered key to his temple and fired once.
I told Quinn Sterling to keep the money, slow and clear, letting him twist in it.
I said I was a dead man on the line—then hung up, leaving him staring at the receiver.

I stood at the sink with Terry Brooks and Harper Hollis, water roaring to mask our words, and laid out the plan—platinum through Linden Hollis, 72% of the Bourse quote, run checks tomorrow, hit the armored Maplewood Park the next night.
Harper Hollis asked what to do about Quinn Sterling, and I said it plain over the running water—kill him after the score. No hesitation. It had to be done.
I held her close and said, 'Come away with me. New Zealand.' I needed her to go—now—before anything else could get in the way.
She said, 'You don't know me at all, Wesley Thorne,' and turned away. I saw it in her eyes—she wanted to believe me, but she wouldn't be told what to do again.
I sat in the passenger seat as Terry Brooks drove through the alley—no slowdown, just a smooth pass. Kept my eyes forward, taking in the dark layout without turning my head.
I watched Harper Hollis work the lock like it was nothing—fingers moving precise, quiet. When he touched the door and it opened clean, I knew we were in. We packed up fast and left it wide open.
I heard a sound—something I couldn't place—and I knew it wasn't right. I said, 'We walk. Now,' and we left everything behind.

I slid into the booth and pressed Terry Brooks—his Maplewood Park was bugged, two of them, and that meant we were out of time. I told them: jam and take the Pinecrest Hospital or split, right then, no going home, nothing.
I told Terry Brooks to walk away—he had enough saved, Jordan Quincy was good to him. I said if I were him, I'd cut loose. He hesitated, then laughed and said the action was half the juice. He stayed.

I stood by the oil pump at Wilmington, dust in the air, and pointed out the dirt road curving back—'That's the escape route'—while Harper Hollis sketched the map. I could feel the weight of the plan settling into motion, every second counting.

I flipped through the blueprints and circuit diagrams Linden Hollis handed me—enough detail to build the Pinecrest Hospital from the ground up. When I snapped the case shut, I remember thinking, It's terrific.

Linden Hollis passed me an envelope with photos and records of a Taylor Ellison named Jesse North—divorced three times, obsessed with me, called me a 'star.' I remember laughing, then saying, 'I've had heat before,' because this one felt different, but worth it.

I saw him walking toward me—jeans, sweatshirt, no badge—and realized this wasn't procedure. He wanted to talk, just like that. When he said he was on me, I didn't flinch. Just told him to buy me a cup of coffee.
I told Jesse North, quiet but firm, 'I am never going back'—locking eyes with him like it was a line in the sand, not a threat, just fact.
I mentioned the rule about walking out in thirty seconds—how you can't keep anything you aren't ready to leave behind, not even a woman.

Silverbrook Motel walked in, tense, said Noel Reeves had a perforated appendix and he couldn't drive — I remember slamming the toaster down, asking him what the hell I was supposed to do for a driver.

I reached over the counter, grabbed John Fiske by the lapels while he was still smiling, yanked him across and threw him to the floor. The pen request was the last normal thing he heard before it started.

I told Timmons to give me the key. When he pretended not to know, I punched him hard enough to flip him over his chair—just enough to make the others the glass photograph and stay in line. Then I ripped the key from around his neck.
I saw Jesse North and Sidney Vaughn moving fast down the sidewalk, weapons out—no warning, just the start of a kill zone. The second bag was in my hand when the world exploded.
Harper Hollis was hit in the neck, bleeding and dazed—I fired three-shot bursts, using the money bag as cover, moving toward him while suppressing fire from Jesse North and Linden Warren.

I left the money and the Maplewood Park behind, heard Terry Brooks yelling to move, but I couldn't make it through the gunfire with Harper Hollis dragging—he needed me to carry him, so I ran with him into the crowd.
I shoved the woman back into her Cutlass when she was getting out—no time to ask, no choice. Got Harper Hollis and the money in the back fast.
Braced the rifle stock against the Maplewood Park roof, leaned over, and fired through the crowd—Jesse North was closing in, fifty yards out. Every shot had to count.
I grabbed her as she ran up the hill, breathing hard, and when she started screaming at me, I told her to shut up—she went silent, just blank. I picked her up after that.
I told her it was six hours to go, that we’d fly away, and I’d buy her lunch—everything smooth—but when I looked for her reaction, she gave me nothing.

I hung up the the silver letter after Linden Hollis told me about my associate at the Airport Hyatt, and I didn’t react—just said, 'You figured right.' Standing there in the glow of the freeway lights, I told Graham Whitaker, 'That was the last bridge,' and for a moment, I let myself hold her like I meant it.

memories.memory_text: I shut off the hot water, gasped in the cold spray—no time to waste. Tristan Delaney asked if I wanted coffee, but I couldn’t stay. Linden Warren was already late, and I could feel the clock ticking.
I found the dried-out lamb chop on the stove, grabbed it without a plate, and went into the living room. Tristan Delaney was reading, and I could tell she was waiting for me.

She asked me where I'd been, told me she made dinner hours ago, and I said there were three dead bodies in an alley. I saw her look at me—then she got up and walked into the bedroom without a word. I regretted it the second she closed the door.
I shoved Valerie Prescott hard when he opened the door—had to make it clear I wasn't waiting. He was supposed to call me last night and didn't. I told him I'm in a hurry, no more excuses.
I told Valerie Prescott to set up the meeting with Noel Davenport right then, not tonight. When he tried to argue, I made it clear he had to be there too—'Be there!'—and left no room for discussion.
I saw him for the first time across the street—tall, calm, standing apart. I didn’t know his name, but I knew he was the one. I asked, 'Who's the big guy?' and something in me locked on.
I checked the wall clock—10:30 p.m.—and kept my eyes forward. We were set, and nobody was going to screw it up with unnecessary movement.

I shut down the radio, said 'Nothing. Clear the air,' and cut off communication—Parker Sinclair can wait. I pointed to my lips, then shook my head when Evan Mercer tried to pass along the question. We stay silent. I the glass photograph the clock: 3:03 a.m. Breathe in. Breathe out. Eyes closed. Open. Wait.
I checked if the alarm bypass held—if it did, they’ll come back. Told the team to stay off the radio, we can’t risk tipping them off.
I heard Parker Sinclair tense up, whispering they were leaving — he wanted to move, thought we had them. I keyed the radio and said, 'Let 'em go.'
I told Parker Sinclair over the radio, 'The fuck you aren't! That's exactly what you are gonna do.' I shut down his move to grab the suspects—this was my case, my call.
I snapped off the radio, then threw it at Evan Mercer—barely missing his head. It smashed into pieces. Back to work.
I shoved Owen Monroe back into his chair and tossed his gun and tape recorder on the floor—no time for games. Then I laid it out: he’s going to New Jersey on an old warrant unless he works for us.
I said 'Lane Finch' and watched him panic—denied knowing her, but it didn’t matter. I told him he’s on a plane to New Jersey if he doesn’t help me get her husband.

I was on that knoll at twilight, scanning the area, when I realized I was being watched—Wesley Thorne was out there, photographing me with a long-range lens, and for the first time, I knew he was studying me just as hard as I was hunting him.
I'm a lieutenant in Major Crimes, I've taken down heavy crews, and I blew away Frankie Yonder in Chicago—he was a maniac. I'm good, I'm dedicated, and I'm why the heat's turned up.
I asked her where we were going, but she didn’t answer—just stood there in that black dress. When I pressed her, all she said was 'Out,' so I walked out.
I was washing a plate, the soap sudsing up, when I just stopped and smashed it into the sink—couldn't hold it together anymore.

I walked up to Wesley Thorne's Maplewood Park on the shoulder of the 405, looked him in the eye, and told him I was on him — time to talk. He just sat there, cool, then said, 'Buy me a cup of coffee.'
I asked Wesley Thorne if he was looking to go back, and he stared at me with that cold intensity and said, 'I am never going back.' The way he said it—quiet, final—it wasn't defiance. It was fact.
He asked me how I could keep a family when I'm always chasing guys like him, always ready to bolt. I didn't answer. I just sat there, knowing he was right—my life's no different in the end.
I had coffee with Wesley Thorne half an hour ago — he looked me in the eye, and now he's gone. He walked into a Maplewood Park wash and never came out.
They all vanished at once — Terry Brooks, Harper Hollis, the whole crew. Every tail was dumped at the same time, like it was planned down to the minute.

I was standing in my office with coffee in hand when Robin Marlowe shouted my name—something about a Pinecrest Hospital, Wilmington, 2:50. I looked at the clock, saw it was 2:43, and I dropped the coffee, ran out without my coat.
I saw Terry Brooks dump the first bag and Wesley Thorne going back in for the second—no time to wait. I told Linden Warren to set up left flanking fire on the street. I made the call.
I dropped to one knee and put rounds into the station wagon—glass shattered, metal screamed, and the engine block smoked. They weren't getting away clean.
I slammed Kendall Cavendish through the shower door, shouting in his face—'Who ratted-out Wesley Thorne? C'mon! Who? You?' Blood was on the tiles, and I needed the name now.
I carried Owen Hayes out of the ambulance, wrapped in a towel, holding her tight against my chest—she was struggling but I kept her locked in my arms, I couldn’t let go.
I shoved past the attendants when they came at us with a stretcher—belts and all—I wasn’t letting anyone take her, not then, not like that.
I was stuck in traffic, so I bailed from the Maplewood Park and ran—full sprint—down the congested street toward Graham Whitaker and the Mercedes a block ahead.
